explainedBy: Sequence start (Brady trains his adult ear): a 32-year-old researcher at his desk with his test notes sets out to test the age cutoff on himself.

storyboard.claim: A 32-year-old Bell Labs researcher, Paul Brady, tested the biological cutoff theory on himself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brady at a lab workstation holding his test notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The Bell Labs case named on the previous beat now appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names him and his age, the fact that makes him a test of the cutoff.

explainedBy: Same stage: Brady starts with an ordinary adult ear, no perfect pitch, and builds his own tone generator.
noVisual: No icon for a 1960s computerized tone generator; the starting point is carried by the face and the label.

storyboard.claim: He had no perfect pitch and built a computerized tone generator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brady, uneasy, at his workstation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; his face turns worried: the starting handicap.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the tone generator itself cannot be drawn.

explainedBy: Same stage, the change: the keyboard of notes appears beside Brady as he drills himself on 12 notes every day for two months.

storyboard.claim: For two months he drilled himself daily on identifying 12 notes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A piano keyboard appears next to Brady with his notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the keyboard (the notes he trains on) is added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows what he is practising: telling musical notes apart.

explainedBy: Same stage: Brady slumps over the keyboard because he practises at the edge of his ability and keeps failing.

storyboard.claim: He kept the test at the edge of his ability, constantly failing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brady slumped and sad beside the keyboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; his body slumps: failure is part of the method.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the discomfort of edge-of-ability practice visible.

explainedBy: Same stage, the turn: after 57 days at the piano the 32-year-old who was supposed to be locked out upends the theory.

storyboard.claim: At 32 his brain should be locked, yet after 57 days on a piano he upended the theory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brady straightens up, surprised, keyboard beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; slump becomes surprise: the result arrives.
storyboard.addedInformation: The 57-day span anchors the turn.

explainedBy: Result: Brady celebrates beside a brain, his adult brain rewired to name notes with near perfect accuracy.

storyboard.claim: He trained his adult ear to near perfect accuracy; his 32-year-old brain rewired.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brady celebrating; the keyboard is replaced by a brain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the object changes from the keyboard to the rewired brain, and he celebrates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the claim is about the adult brain changing.

explainedBy: Comparison: casual listening to the radio versus a hard, unfamiliar state that forces the brain to adapt; only the second changed him.

storyboard.claim: He didn't casually listen to music; he forced his brain into a difficult state where it had to adapt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two buckets: casual radio listening vs forced adaptation.
storyboard.onScreenText: Beatles on the radio | Forced to adapt
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the result to why it worked.
storyboard.addedInformation: Separates the two kinds of exposure the narration contrasts.

explainedBy: Comparison: the Tokyo three-year-old and the 32-year-old Brady side by side at the same keyboard, one rule for both.

storyboard.claim: Whether 3 in Tokyo or 32 at Bell Labs, the rule is the same: comfort is where improvement stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The toddler and Brady together beside a piano keyboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Joins the earlier Tokyo case to Brady's.
storyboard.addedInformation: The child and the adult on one stage make 'any age' visible.

explainedBy: Back to the lab and the runner who pushed his memory to failure: the stopwatch of his story.
noVisual: 'Push the tissue to failure' is a metaphor with no literal object; the strained runner carries it.

storyboard.claim: You have to push to failure, which brings us back to the college student.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve, the red-jacket runner, slumped with strain at the lab desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Brady back to Steve's memory study.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: reintroduces Steve; the idea itself is text-led.

explainedBy: Back in the lab: the runner and the researcher at the stopwatch, stuck at eight digits.

storyboard.claim: Back in the lab, Steve had hit the wall at eight digits before jumping much higher.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve and the mustached researcher face each other at the lab table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the scene in the testing room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the tester and the subject together, the setup of the test.

explainedBy: Same stage: the researcher reads out dozens of numbers for 40 timed seconds while Steve listens, tense.

storyboard.claim: Silence for a 40-second recitation as the researcher reads dozens of numbers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher talks; a stopwatch runs; Steve listens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the researcher starts talking and the stopwatch appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stopwatch shows the timed reading.

explainedBy: Same stage, the change: Steve slaps the table and yells the whole string back in fierce focus; the researcher is taken aback.
noVisual: The table slap itself is not an action in the rig; the yelling face and the label carry it.

storyboard.claim: Steve slaps the table in aggressive focus and yells out the string of numbers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve shouting with a fierce face; the researcher surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; Steve goes from listening to shouting, the researcher stops reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the intensity of the recall.

explainedBy: Result: Steve celebrates his certainty after the recall, though, as the hosts add, his memory did not physically grow.

storyboard.claim: He shouts 'Absolutely right, I'm certain'; his short-term memory did not magically grow.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve celebrating, the researcher still surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; fierce focus turns into triumph; the stopwatch is gone.
storyboard.addedInformation: His own words show the confidence of the recall.

explainedBy: A brain with the famous limit: George Miller's finding that short-term memory holds about seven items, plus or minus two.

storyboard.claim: In the 1950s George Miller showed short-term memory holds about seven items, plus or minus two.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A brain with the label 'seven, plus or minus two'.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Steve's feat to the known limit he faced.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the number of the limit.

explainedBy: Same brain: that limit is still biologically true; short-term memory cannot be stretched like a balloon.
noVisual: No icon for a balloon or a fixed capacity; the kept brain plus the label carry it.

storyboard.claim: That limit is still true; you cannot stretch short-term memory like a balloon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same brain stays on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept brain; the label changes from the number to 'cannot stretch'.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: only the label changes.

explainedBy: Sequence start (the running-time trick): Steve grabs an idea drawn from his running, the stopwatch, to get around his short-term memory.

storyboard.claim: Under pressure Steve invented strategies to bypass short-term memory, using his running background.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve takes a lightbulb (an idea) beside a running stopwatch.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the fixed limit to how he went around it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Links the trick to running times via the stopwatch.

explainedBy: Same stage: the resourceful runner hears a string of numbers such as 9, 0, 7.

storyboard.claim: The brain is resourceful: he heard a string of numbers like 9-0-7.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve holding the idea, stopwatch beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the example digits arrive in the label.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the concrete example the trick will use.

explainedBy: Steve has an idea (the lightbulb): he will not hold the digits as random numbers but as a running time on the stopwatch.

storyboard.claim: He didn't memorize 907 as three random digits.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve with a knowing look; 'three random digits' struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; his face turns knowing, the naive reading is crossed out.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike shows the rejected method.

explainedBy: Mechanism: the digits 907 are translated into a two-mile running time, 9 minutes 7 seconds.

storyboard.claim: He translated 907 into a two-mile running time, routing it into long-term memory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow from the digits to the running time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the person to the mechanism of his trick.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the conversion step itself.

explainedBy: Same flow, one more step: the familiar running time anchors the fragile new digits in long-term memory.

storyboard.claim: He used existing pathways, his knowledge of running times, to anchor the new information.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains a third step: long-term memory.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; one label added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes the route: digits -> known time -> memory.

explainedBy: Steve with his digit notes, worried: the running trick alone could not carry him to 82 digits.

storyboard.claim: Even that trick wasn't enough for 82 digits; another test subject shows the limits of tricks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve looking worried at his notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The trick hits its limit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the comparison with a second subject.

explainedBy: Sequence start (Renee's random tricks): Renee Elio, same task and hours, slumps at a wall of 20 digits.

storyboard.claim: Renee Elio did the same task and hours but hit a wall at 20 digits.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Renee, green turtleneck, slumped over her notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Steve to a second subject.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Renee and her limit.

explainedBy: Same stage: Renee keeps inventing a new disconnected memory trick for each string, one second a historical date.
noVisual: Her shifting mnemonics have no object; the label names them.

storyboard.claim: She stopped at 20 because she invented random, disconnected mnemonics, like a historical date.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Renee worried, muttering over her notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; she lifts from the slump and tries again.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the cause of her wall.

explainedBy: Result: date, then time of day, then phone number; with no system, Renee slumps again.

storyboard.claim: The next string was a time of day, then a phone number; there was no system.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Renee slumps back over her notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; she slumps again: the attempts go nowhere.
storyboard.addedInformation: States what she lacked.

explainedBy: Sequence start (the retrieval tree): Steve points to a tree, the fixed retrieval structure he built by trial and error.

storyboard.claim: Steve had built a fixed retrieval structure, like a filing cabinet or a tree with branches.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve pointing at a tree.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Renee's lack to what Steve had.
storyboard.addedInformation: The tree is the narration's own image for the structure.

callout.text: Which branch the digits hang on

explainedBy: Same tree: Steve knew which branch the first three digits hung on and which the next four did.

storyboard.claim: He knew exactly which branch each group of digits would hang on.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve explaining beside the tree.
storyboard.onScreenText: Which branch the digits hang on
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; he goes from pointing to explaining the branches.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains how the tree is used.

explainedBy: Same tree, the test of it: the structure stays fixed, and a third runner, Dario Donatelli, walks in to learn it.

storyboard.claim: The structure was permanent, only the numbers changed; then a third runner, Dario Donatelli, was brought in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dario in a blue track jacket walks in beside Steve and the tree.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; Dario enters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the proof case.

explainedBy: Result: taught Steve's exact tree, Dario celebrates passing 100 digits while Steve looks on, surprised, at his record broken.

storyboard.claim: Taught Steve's exact retrieval structure, Dario shattered Steve's record and passed 100 digits.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dario celebrating by the tree, Steve surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; Dario celebrates, Steve is surprised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the structure, not the person, made the record.

callout.text: The structure, not raw brain power

explainedBy: The host states the lesson beside the tree (structure beats raw brain power), then raises a doubt about Steve's genes.

storyboard.claim: It's the structure that matters, not raw brain power; but was Steve genetically gifted after all?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host talking beside the tree.
storyboard.onScreenText: The structure, not raw brain power
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the lab story to the hosts' debate.
storyboard.addedInformation: Restates the conclusion before the pushback.

explainedBy: Steve the long-distance runner, logging miles against the clock.
noVisual: No rain or weather icon is allowed for this book; the running figure and the label carry the hardship.

storyboard.claim: He was a competitive distance runner, used to logging miles in freezing rain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve moving down a street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pushback: look at who Steve was.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hardship the argument rests on.

explainedBy: Same stage: Steve walks on through it while Renee slumps; the claim is that he had a tolerance for suffering she lacked.
noVisual: No rain or weather icon is allowed for this book; the running figure and the label carry the hardship.

storyboard.claim: He had an innate tolerance for pain, boredom and repetitive suffering that Renee lacked.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve walking calmly; Renee slumped beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; Renee is added as the contrast, Steve's face calms.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the comparison between the two subjects visible.

explainedBy: The host restates the challenge as a question: maybe grit, not memory, is the inborn gift.
noVisual: A hosts' hypothesis; nothing in the vocabulary shows 'grit as a gene'.

storyboard.claim: So grit is the gift; maybe his memory wasn't larger.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host asking the question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the example back to the debate.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: commentary, carried by the question.

explainedBy: The objection: maybe grit itself is an inborn gift.
noVisual: A hypothetical about genes; no literal object.

storyboard.claim: Isn't that grit a genetic talent? Aren't some people wired for suffering?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host, troubled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; her face turns troubled.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: text-led question.

explainedBy: Comparison: labelling grit an inherited gene versus Ericsson's environmental explanation.

storyboard.claim: It's tempting to call grit an inherited gene, but Ericsson points to the environment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two buckets: inherited gene vs environmental reality.
storyboard.onScreenText: A magical inherited gene | Environmental reality
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The answer to the pushback.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lays out the two explanations side by side.

explainedBy: Sequence start (the feedback loop): motivation comes from his setting; Steve takes his hourly pay from the researcher.

storyboard.claim: Motivation is a feedback loop: Steve was paid by the hour and saw his scores rise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve takes a coin, the researcher beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the theory to Steve's actual environment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the first reward feeding his drive.

explainedBy: Same stage: Steve sees his scores climb on the chart every day and celebrates; he is becoming a campus celebrity.

storyboard.claim: Daily rising scores gave him a dopamine hit; he became a minor celebrity on campus.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve celebrating, the researcher smiling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; Steve celebrates and the researcher is pleased.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the daily reward.

explainedBy: Steve in front of a TV camera on the Today Show: the social reward that makes grit a byproduct of the loop.

storyboard.claim: His success landed him on the Today Show; when feedback is that rewarding, grit is the byproduct.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve talking to a video camera on a stage.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the lab to television.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows how far the social reward went.

explainedBy: Cause and effect: the tight, rewarding feedback loop produces grit; grit is the result, not the genetic root.

storyboard.claim: Grit is the byproduct, not the genetic root cause; his loop was built on breaking his own systems.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: tight feedback loop -> grit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the mechanism behind the rewards just shown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reverses the cause the pushback assumed.

explainedBy: Sequence start (breaking the plateau): Steve slumps over his notes, stuck at 22 digits as his three-digit groups fail.

storyboard.claim: It wasn't smooth: he hit a plateau at 22 digits and his groupings were failing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve slumped over his notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the rewards to the setback.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows progress stalling.

explainedBy: Mechanism: trying harder fails, so he tears down the old digit groups and rebuilds them as a new mix.

storyboard.claim: He couldn't just try harder; he had to tear down and rebuild his mental architecture.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow from old digit groups to a new three- and four-digit mix.
storyboard.onScreenText: Old digit groups -> Three- and four-digit mix
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the stall to the fix.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows what changed in his method.

explainedBy: Same flow, the result: the new three- and four-digit mix breaks the plateau.

storyboard.claim: A complex mix of three- and four-digit groups broke the plateau.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains its result: plateau broken.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; one label added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes cause -> change -> result.
